newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian Interior Minister tangled in drug probe.
newsitem.headline: Colombian Interior Minister tangled in drug probe.

text.p: Colombian Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, a likely presidential candidate next year, learned on Thursday that he may be headed for jail instead.

Serpa, President Ernesto Samper's right-hand man, is the target of an investigation into charges that he knew about and helped cover up the alleged use of millions of dollars in drug money to finance Samper's 1994 campaign.

The probe was shelved on a technicality in September, but chief prosecutor Alfonso Valdivieso reopened it and issued a restraining order against Serpa late on Wednesday in a move judicial officials said sent a strong signal that there was sufficient evidence to keep the case open and press for Serpa's prosecution on cover-up and fraud charges.

Evidence includes testimony from Samper's former campaign manager and defence minister Fernando Botero, son of the painter and sculptor of the same name, who has been held at a military base since August 1995 on drug corruption charges.

Spokesmen for Valdivieso, who was in Switzerland to address the World Economic Forum, said he had ordered Serpa to notify the prosecutor-general's office of any plans to leave the country or change his place of residence. The order also requires Serpa to observe strict good conduct in public.

Serpa, who said he learned of the restraining order by listening to morning radio news programmes, said it was something his detractors were sure to exploit politically and seek to humiliate him with in public.
"I'm very worried," he said in an interview with the Caracol radio network. "This news saddens me a lot."

Samper himself was cleared by the lower house of Congress last year of charges that he received up to $6 million in contributions from the Cali drug cartel to help bankroll his campaign. The charges, which triggered Colombia's worst political crisis in decades, were brought by Valdivieso, an anti-drug crusader who is in favour in Washington.
His pursuit of the case against Serpa, a staunch Semper supporter and firebrand populist, raises possible conflict of interest questions that Serpa has not addressed in public.

Polls show Valdivieso as the front-runner to succeed Samper, whose term ends in August 1998. But he has indicated he may not run for the country's top job, and that would leave Serpa as the front-runner, if elections were held today.
